title: DarkSeoul — the wiper that came before Sony

scenes.label: 2 p.m. in Seoul: the screens die
scenes.narration: [dramatically] One afternoon, a hidden timer killed thousands of computers across South Korea. [short pause] [serious] It's Wednesday, March 20, 2013, in Seoul. It's 2 in the afternoon. At big banks and major TV stations, screens freeze. Machines restart, and they never come back. One reporter takes a photo of a dead screen. It shows one cold line. [slowly] Boot device not found. [short pause] [curious] So who set that timer? And how? To find out, we have to go back almost a year.

scenes.label: A country that lives online
scenes.narration: [calmly] First, picture South Korea back then. It's one of the most connected countries on Earth. People pay with cards. They bank on their phones. They get their news from big TV networks like KBS and MBC. Big banks like Shinhan and NongHyup handle people's money all day long. All of it runs on computers that most people never think about. [short pause] [ominously] But just across the border, someone was thinking about them a lot.

visuals.at: All of it runs on computers

scenes.label: June 2012: the quiet start
scenes.narration: [curious] That someone was North Korea. At least, that's what South Korean investigators would later say. They say the planning started in June 2012. Nobody in Seoul noticed a thing. In the months before the attack, workers got emails that looked normal. But they weren't normal. They were bait. Security company McAfee later found that emails like these planted back doors. A back door is a secret way into a computer. [whispers] The attackers were inside. And they were waiting.

scenes.label: A dangerous winter and a timer
scenes.narration: [serious] Then came early 2013. Things between the two Koreas got very tense. In February, North Korea tested a nuclear weapon. Soon after, it said the deal that stopped the Korean War in 1953 was no longer valid. It was even threatening the United States. That same February, investigators say, North Korean computers ran a test of the attack. Like a fire drill. [short pause] Then someone set the timer. The date? March 20. The time? 2 in the afternoon.

visuals.at: ran a test of the attack

scenes.label: The safety tool that turned
scenes.narration: [cautiously] But how do you hit thousands of computers at the same moment? The attackers found a clever shortcut. Big companies use special software to send updates to all their computers at once. In some places, that software came from AhnLab, a Korean security company. The attackers used stolen usernames and passwords to get into it. [short pause] Think about that. The tool meant to keep computers safe would now deliver the bomb. It even tried to switch off antivirus programs first.

scenes.label: 2 p.m.: the wipe begins
scenes.narration: [dramatically] March 20. The clock hits 2. The timer goes off. [short pause] The program is a wiper. That means it doesn't steal. It destroys. It erases the small part of a hard drive that tells a computer how to start up. Without it, the machine is just a dead box. Researchers at Sophos found it wrote one strange word over and over. Hastati. It's an old name for soldiers in ancient Rome's army. [serious] And it didn't just hit desk computers. It went after big servers too.

visuals.at: small part of a hard drive

scenes.label: Frozen ATMs, dark newsrooms
scenes.narration: [worried] Out on the streets, people felt it fast. At Shinhan Bank, online banking and ATMs went down for about two hours. Cash machines froze in other places too. At one Starbucks in downtown Seoul, people were asked to pay in cash. Inside the TV stations, it was just as bad. Staff at KBS, MBC and YTN, a news channel, couldn't log in to their news systems. [short pause] Oddly, the shows stayed on the air. [nervous] But who was doing this?

scenes.label: Skulls on the homepage
scenes.narration: [curious] That same afternoon, a strange answer popped up. The website of LG U+, a big Korean internet company, was taken over. It showed skulls. It played the sound of laughter. A group called the Whois Team said they did it. Their message said: [softly] This is the beginning of our movement. [short pause] Unfortunately, we have deleted your data. We'll be back soon. [serious] It looked like a silly prank by show-offs. Some experts thought so too. They were wrong.

visuals.text: "This is the beginning of our movement."

scenes.label: 48,000 computers wiped
scenes.narration: [serious] Over the next days, the damage got clearer. At first, officials counted about 32,000 broken computers. Then the number kept going up. In the end, investigators said 48,000 computers and servers were hit. That's more than every seat at Yankee Stadium. Some banks had trouble for two to five days. [short pause] There was one piece of good news. Officials said no bank records or personal data were taken. [slowly] This attack wasn't about money. It was about chaos.

scenes.label: The China clue that wasn't
scenes.narration: [nervous] Now everyone wanted a name. And on March 21, the day after the attack, it looked like they had one. South Korea's internet watchdog said the bad code came from an address in China. The news spread fast. [short pause] Then officials took it back. The address wasn't in China at all. It belonged to NongHyup Bank's own network. Someone had misread it in the rush. [sighs] It showed how hard it is to catch a hacker. Clues can lie.

scenes.label: They came back for more
scenes.narration: [worried] And the attackers weren't done. Just days later, on March 25 and 26, a second wave hit. It struck dozens of servers and more than a dozen websites. Some of those sites were run by people who had escaped from North Korea. Meanwhile, investigators dug through mountains of clues. They found more than 1,000 internet addresses spread across 40 countries. [short pause] The trail went all over the world. [curious] But where did it really start?

scenes.label: April 10: Seoul names a suspect
scenes.narration: [serious] On April 10, 2013, South Korean officials stood up in front of reporters. They named North Korea. They said a spy agency run by the North's military was behind it. Here's why. Many of the harmful programs had been used before, in older attacks. And North Korean systems had reached into South Korean networks at least 13 times. Chun Kil-soo, from Korea's internet security agency, put it simply. [slowly] We saw evidence that the attack was extremely carefully prepared.

visuals.at: stood up in front of reporters

scenes.label: Years in the shadows
scenes.narration: [curious] Private security companies kept digging. And the story got bigger. Symantec gave the hackers a name: the DarkSeoul gang. It linked them to about four years of attacks on South Korea. Many of them hit on dates that meant something. On June 25, 2013, the anniversary of the start of the Korean War, government websites were attacked again. Symantec tied one of those attacks to the same gang. McAfee found spying on South Korea's military going back to at least 2009. [ominously] The wipe was just the loud part.

visuals.at: the start of the Korean War

scenes.label: The road to Hollywood
scenes.narration: [deep voice] Now jump ahead to November 2014. Sony Pictures, the Hollywood movie studio, gets hacked. A wiper erases its computers. On December 19, the FBI says North Korea's government did it. And the FBI points straight back to Seoul. It says the tools used on Sony were like the ones used that March against South Korean banks and TV stations. [short pause] In 2016, a group of security companies tied both attacks to one team of hackers. Today, they're known as Lazarus.

scenes.label: The warning nobody heard
scenes.narration: [reflective] Here's what makes this story so chilling. Almost everything from the Sony hack happened in Seoul first. The quiet break-in. The fake hacker group. The skulls on a screen. The timer set to the minute. At the time, an American cybersecurity expert named James Barnett gave a warning. [serious] This needs to be a wake-up call. This can happen anywhere. [long pause] [softly] Most of the world didn't wake up. Not until it hit Hollywood. If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

visuals.at: The timer set to the minute

facts.claim: Computers at South Korean banks and broadcasters went down at 2 p.m. local time on Wednesday, March 20, 2013.
A KBS World Radio reporter photographed a screen reading 'Boot device not found. Please install an operating system on your hard disk.'
Victims included KBS, MBC, YTN, Shinhan Bank, NongHyup Bank, Jeju Bank and insurance affiliates.
Shinhan Bank had a roughly two-hour shutdown including online banking and ATMs; a downtown Seoul Starbucks asked customers to pay cash; TV broadcasts were not affected.
North Korea had tested a nuclear weapon a month earlier and revoked the 1953 armistice; a defense ministry spokesman said it was premature to blame the North.
LG U+ homepage replaced with skulls, laughter and lightning effects and a Whois Team message 'an interest in hacking' / 'beginning of our movement'.
Whois Team video: 'Unfortunately, We have deleted your data. We'll be back soon.'

Wipers overwrote the MBR with repeated 'HASTATI.' or 'PRINCPES' strings, names of Roman battle-line units; one variant waited until March 20, 2013 14:00; tried to kill AhnLab and Hauri processes; forced reboot; a companion script targeted Linux/Unix servers.
AhnLab ASEC found attackers distributed malware through patch management software.
Spear-phishing emails in the three months before the attack installed back doors (McAfee).
Initial estimate about 32,000 computers; later 48,000 PCs and servers.

Banks hampered two to five days; broadcasters' staff couldn't access news systems for several days; no bank records or personal data compromised; 76 malware programs, 30 recycled; 1,000+ IPs in 40 countries; planned about eight months; quote 'extremely carefully prepared'.
On March 21, 2013 the Korea Communications Commission traced code to a Chinese IP; later retracted as a NongHyup private IP address.

Second wave March 25-26 targeted 58 servers and 14 websites including North Korean defector sites; planning from June 2012; February 2013 test; 13 direct accesses from North Korean systems; Reconnaissance General Bureau methods.
South Korea announced North Korea attribution on April 10, 2013.
Symantec tied the DarkSeoul gang to about four years of attacks, including a June 25, 2013 DDoS on the 63rd Korean War anniversary.
McAfee's Operation Troy dates to at least 2009 and aimed to spy on South Korea's military.
FBI on December 19, 2014 said Sony malware was similar to tools used in a March 2013 cyberattack against South Korean banks and media outlets.
Operation Blockbuster (February 2016) linked DarkSeoul and the Sony attack to the Lazarus Group.
James Barnett of Venable: 'This needs to be a wake-up call. This can happen anywhere.'
Malware was spread through AhnLab's enterprise patch management software at some targeted sites, using stolen legitimate usernames and passwords; some systems carried a logic bomb set for March 20.
Chun Kil-soo of the Korea Internet Security Agency: 'We saw evidence that the attack was extremely carefully prepared.'
Operation Blockbuster (announced February 25, 2016) connected malware used in Operation DarkSeoul and Operation Troy to the Lazarus Group, believed to be behind the 2014 Sony Pictures attack.
Yankee Stadium seats about 46,500 people, fewer than the 48,000 machines hit.

seo.youtube_description:
How South Korea was hacked: the true story of DarkSeoul, the cyberattack that wiped 48,000 computers at banks and TV stations at exactly 2 p.m. on March 20, 2013.
It looked like a prank. It was months in the making, and it was a warning before the Sony Pictures hack.

On March 20, 2013, ATMs froze in Seoul and newsrooms at KBS, MBC and YTN went dark. A group calling itself the Whois Team put skulls on an internet company's homepage. But investigators found something far bigger: planning that started in June 2012, fake emails that opened secret back doors, and a trusted software-update tool turned into a delivery truck for a timed wiper.

In April 2013, South Korea blamed North Korea's military spy agency. Researchers later tied the DarkSeoul gang to years of attacks. In December 2014, the FBI pointed back to this attack when it blamed North Korea for hacking Sony Pictures. This hacking documentary tells the whole story in plain English, using only public records and news reports.
